title: Conquer yourself (103–108)
hookLine: one who conquers himself is greater than one who conquers a thousand times a thousand in battle

cards: The Buddha grew up among warriors. Born into a ruling family and trained, the stories say, in the arts of a prince, he lived among kings who measured greatness by battles won and lands taken.
In that world, a conqueror meant one thing. So when he described the greatest victory a person could win, he borrowed their language, and then turned it completely around.

teach.h: A MILLION ENEMIES, OR ONE SELF.
teach.b: Verse one hundred three, in Müller's English: “If one man conquer in battle a thousand times thousand men, and if another conquer himself, he is the greatest of conquerors.” A thousand times a thousand: a million enemies.
Or one person, sitting quietly, who has won against their own anger, their own craving, their own fog. The verse calls that second person the greater conqueror.

teach.h: A VICTORY NO ONE CAN UNDO.
teach.b: Verses one hundred four and one hundred five say why: no one can take that victory back. Not a god, not a heavenly musician, not Mara, not even Brahma, can turn it into defeat.
A king's victories can be undone in a single battle. Land is lost, alliances break, the next king comes. But a mind that has truly let go of hatred doesn't have to win that fight again.

teach.h: A MOMENT OVER A HUNDRED YEARS.
teach.b: Verses one hundred six to one hundred eight add a surprise: a hundred years of ritual sacrifice is worth less than honoring, for a single moment, one person whose mind is well trained.
And this conquest needn't be dramatic.
It's small, daily, mostly invisible. Not snapping at your kid. Putting the phone down.
Letting a grudge go for the fourth time this week.
Nobody writes songs about those battles. One of the Buddha's titles carries the same idea: the Jina, the conqueror. Not of lands.

how: Buddhist teachers often quote verse one hundred three to describe practice as an inner victory, and 'Jina,' the conqueror, is one of the traditional titles of the Buddha.

o: winning over your own anger and craving
beating every rival who stands in your way
punishing yourself hard for every failure

games.q: match the pieces of verses one hundred three to one hundred eight.
p: the conqueror, a title of the Buddha

s: verse one hundred three praises the king who wins the most battles
it says the one who conquers himself is the greatest of conquerors.
verses one hundred four and one hundred five say no god can undo victory over oneself
not a god, a heavenly musician, Mara or Brahma.
Jina, the conqueror, is a title of the Buddha
Jains use the same title for their great teachers.

games.q: someone says something sharp to you in a meeting. the reply is already on your tongue. what would the greatest conqueror do?
o: pause for one breath before answering.
say nothing now and win it later by email.
games.why: the conquest the verse praises is inner: the breath before the reply is the battle, and it's the one that can't be undone.

practice: Think of one small inner fight you keep losing: reaching for the phone, the sharp reply, the second helping you don't want, the spiral of worry at night.
Picture the moment it usually starts, the first itch or flare, and see yourself noticing it and pausing for one breath before acting.
That pause is the whole battle, nothing heroic; rest here and let the body feel what it's like to win it.

wordCard.voice: Conquer yourself. One who wins over their own mind is greater than one who conquers a million in battle, and that victory can't be undone.

orig.note: Pali: conqueror, a title of the Buddha, the one who conquered himself.

carryVoice: Your line: the greatest conquest. A victory no one can take back. Day one hundred seventy-nine, done.

sources.q: If one man conquer in battle a thousand times thousand men, and if another conquer himself, he is the greatest of conquerors.
